Registers
In common with other Austronesian languages, Javanese is spoken differently depending on the social context. In
Austronesian languages there are often three distinct styles or <color=#3366CC>registers</color>. Each employs its own vocabulary,
grammatical rules, and even <color=#3366CC>prosody</color>. In Javanese these styles are called:
• Ngoko: Vernacular or informal speech, used between friends and close relatives. It is also used by persons of
higher status (such as elders, or bosses) addressing those of lower status (young people, or subordinates in the
workplace).
• Madya: Intermediate between ngoko and krama. Strangers on the street would use it, where status differences
may be unknown and one wants to be neither too formal nor too informal. The term is from Sanskrit madhya
("middle").
• Krama: The polite, high-register, or formal style. It is used between those of the same status when they do not wish
to be informal. It is used by persons of lower status to persons of higher status, such as young people to their
elders, or subordinates to bosses; and it is the official style for public speeches, announcements, etc. The term is
from Sanskrit krama ("in order").
There are also "meta-style" <color=#3366CC>honorific</color> words, and their converse "humilifics". Speakers use "humble" words concerning
themselves, but honorific words concerning anyone of greater age or higher social status. The humilific words are
called krama andhap, while the honorifics are called krama inggil. This honorific system is very similar to that of the
Japanese keigo. Children typically use the ngoko style, but in talking to the parents they must be competent with both
krama inggil and krama andhap.
The most polite word meaning "eat" is dhahar. But it is considered inappropriate to use these most polite words for
oneself, except when talking with someone of lower status; and in this case, ngoko style is used. Such most polite
words are reserved for addressing people of higher status:
• Mixed usages
• (honorific – addressing someone of high status) Bapak kersa dhahar? ("Do you want to eat?"; literally "Does father
want to eat?")
• (reply to a person of lower status, expressing speaker's superiority) Iya, aku kersa dhahar. ("Yes, I want to eat.")
• (reply to a person of lower status, but without expressing superiority) Iya, aku arep mangan.
• (reply to a person of equal status) Inggih, kula badhé nedha.
The use of these different styles is complicated and requires thorough knowledge of Javanese culture, which adds to
the difficulty of Javanese for foreigners. The full system is not usually mastered by most Javanese themselves, who
might use only the ngoko and a rudimentary form of the krama. People who can correctly use the different styles are
held in high esteem.
Sample text
The following is a sample text in Javanese of Article 1 of the <color=#3366CC>Universal Declaration of Human Rights</color>.
Italians
Italians (Italian: italiani) are an <color=#3366CC>ethnic group</color> and <color=#3366CC>nation</color> native to the Italian geographical region. Italians share a

common <color=#3366CC>culture</color>, <color=#3366CC>history</color>, <color=#3366CC>ancestry</color> and <color=#3366CC>language</color>. Their ancestors, differing regionally, include the various Italic peoples,
notably among them the ancient Romans, who helped create and evolve the Italian identity. The Latin equivalent of the
term Italian had been in use for natives of the geographical region since <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color>. Ethnic Italians (a group which
includes people of Italian descent without Italian citizenship) can be distinguished from Italian nationals, who are
citizens of <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> regardless of ancestry or nation of residence.
The majority of Italian nationals are native speakers of the country's official language, <color=#3366CC>Standard Italian</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Romance</color>
<color=#3366CC>language</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Indo-European language family</color> that evolved from the <color=#3366CC>Vulgar Latin</color>. However, many of them also speak
a regional or minority language native to Italy, the existence of which predates the national language of Standard
Italian. (According to <color=#3366CC>UNESCO</color>, there are approximately 30 languages native to Italy, although many are often
incorrectly referred to as "Italian <color=#3366CC>dialects</color>".)
In addition to the approximately 55 million Italians living in Italy (91% of the Italian national population), Italian-speaking
groups are found in neighboring nations, including Switzerland, France, the regions of Istria and Dalmatia, and the
entire population of <color=#3366CC>San Marino</color>. Due to the wide-ranging diaspora of Italians following <color=#3366CC>Italian unification</color>, <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, over 5 million Italian citizens live outside of Italy and over 80 million people around the world claim
full or partial Italian ancestry. The largest Italian diaspora communities are found in Brazil (15% of Brazilians), Argentina
(60% of <color=#3366CC>Argentinians</color>), the United States, and Canada.

Italians have influenced and contributed to fields like arts and <color=#3366CC>music</color>, <color=#3366CC>science</color>, <color=#3366CC>technology</color>, fashion, <color=#3366CC>cinema</color>, <color=#3366CC>cuisine</color>,

<color=#3366CC>restaurants</color>, <color=#3366CC>sports</color>, <color=#3366CC>jurisprudence</color>, <color=#3366CC>banking</color> and <color=#3366CC>business</color>. Furthermore, Italian people are generally known for their
attachment to their locale, expressed in the form of either regionalism or municipalism.
Name
The Latin name "Italia" may have been borrowed via <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> from the Oscan Víteliú ("land of calves"). Accounts by
Dionysius of Halicarnassus, <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Thucydides</color> reference this etymology, together with the legend that Italy was
named after legendary King Italus. According to Antiochus of Syracuse, the Greeks initially used the term Italy to refer
only to the southern portion of the Bruttium peninsula (corresponding to parts of the modern provinces of <color=#3366CC>Reggio</color>,
Catanzaro, and Vibo Valentia); however, over time, the Greeks gradually came to apply the name "Italia" to a larger
region including Lucania and <color=#3366CC>Calabria</color>.
Roman historian <color=#3366CC>Cato the Elder</color> described Italy as the entire peninsula south of the <color=#3366CC>Alps</color>, which he said formed the
"walls of Italy". In the 260s BCE, Roman Italy extended from the Arno and Rubicon rivers to the entire south. The
northern area of Cisalpine Gaul was occupied by Rome in the 220s BC and became considered geographically and de
facto part of Italy, but remained politically and de jure separated until <color=#3366CC>Octavian</color> legally merged it into the administrative
unit of Italy in 42 BCE. Under Emperor <color=#3366CC>Diocletian</color>, Italy was further enlarged to include the three big islands of the

western <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>: <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> (with the Maltese archipelago), <color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Corsica</color>. All its inhabitants were
considered Italic and Roman.
The Latin term Italicus was used to describe "a man of Italy" as opposed to a provincial from the greater Roman
provinces. The Greeks likewise used terms such as (Italikoi) and (Italiotes) to refer to the peoples and inhabitants of
Italy. The adjective Italianus emerged in the <color=#3366CC>medieval period</color> and was used as an alternative alongside Italicus into the
<color=#3366CC>early modern period</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Italy</color> was created after the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color>. The name "Italia" was retained for the
kingdom under the <color=#3366CC>Lombards</color> and later their successor kingdom within the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>.
History
Roman era
The <color=#3366CC>Italian peninsula</color> was divided into multiple tribal or ethnic territories prior to the <color=#3366CC>Roman conquest of Italy</color> in the 3rd
century BCE. The Latins, with <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> as their capital, came to dominate the Italian peninsula by 218 BCE. They
continued to expand beyond Italy, and after a <color=#3366CC>century-long struggle</color> against <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color>, Rome conquered Sicily,
Sardinia, and Corsica. By the end of the <color=#3366CC>Third Punic War</color> in 146 BCE, Rome had completely destroyed Carthage and
become the dominant power in the Mediterranean. Unification and Romanization of Italy culminated in 88 BC, when, in
the aftermath of the Social War, Rome granted Roman citizenship to all fellow Italic peoples.
Rome was originally a republican city-state, but four famous civil conflicts destroyed the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color>: <color=#3366CC>Sulla</color> against

<color=#3366CC>Marius</color> (88–82 BCE), <color=#3366CC>Julius Caesar</color> against <color=#3366CC>Pompey</color> (49–45 BC), <color=#3366CC>Brutus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Cassius</color> against <color=#3366CC>Mark Antony</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Octavian</color> (43 BC), and Mark Antony against Octavian. Octavian, the final victor (31 BC), became the first Roman
Emperor.
During the <color=#3366CC>Crisis of the Third Century</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> nearly collapsed under the combined pressures of invasions,
civil wars, and hyperinflation. In 284 CE, Emperor <color=#3366CC>Diocletian</color> restored political stability. He divided the Roman Empire's
territory and administration into the <color=#3366CC>Western</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> Empires. Christianity became the Roman state religion in AD
380, under Emperor <color=#3366CC>Theodosius I</color>. The defeat of the last Western Roman emperor, <color=#3366CC>Romulus Augustulus</color>, by Germanic
general <color=#3366CC>Odoacer</color> marked the end of the Western Roman Empire (and political unification of Italy until the establishment
of the modern Kingdom of Italy in 1861).
The Middle Ages
<color=#3366CC>Odoacer</color> ruled as the first king of Italy. After the death of his successor <color=#3366CC>Theodoric</color> in 526 CE, the kingdom began to
grow weak. By 553 CE, Byzantine Emperor <color=#3366CC>Justinian I</color> expelled the Ostrogoths from Italy and brought it back under
Roman control. However, within twenty years, the <color=#3366CC>Lombards</color> invaded Italy and conquered most of the peninsula.
(Remnants of Byzantine control remained in Southern Italy until the Arab conquest of <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> in the 9th century and the
<color=#3366CC>Norman conquest of Southern Italy</color> in the 11th; the interaction among Latin, Byzantine, Arab, and Norman cultures
resulted in the formation of a unique Norman-Arab-Byzantine culture in Southern Italy.)
For two centuries following the Lombard invasion, the <color=#3366CC>popes</color> opposed foreign rule in Italy. They ultimately defeated the
Lombards, with the aid of two Frankish kings, <color=#3366CC>Pepin</color> and <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>, and established the <color=#3366CC>Papal States</color> in central Italy
in 756. To cement the Church's alliance with Charlemagne, <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo III</color> crowned him the Roman Emperor in 800.
Members of the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian dynasty</color> continued to rule Italy, and this Kingdom of Italy became part of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> in the 10th century.
The Renaissance and the Age of Discovery
From the 11th century on, Italian cities rapidly grew in independence and importance, becoming centers of political life,

<color=#3366CC>banking</color>, and foreign trade. Many, including <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Milan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pisa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Siena</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>, grew into nearly
independent city-states and <color=#3366CC>maritime republics</color>, each with its own foreign policy and trade. By the 14th and 15th
centuries, some Italian city-states, such as Venice and Florence, ranked among the most influential powers in Europe.
The Italian merchant cities acted as a gateway for goods and ideas from the Byzantine and <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color> world into Europe;
the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> began in Florence in the 14th century and led to an unparalleled flourishing of the arts, literature,
music, and science.
Italian explorers and navigators, eager to find alternative trade routes to the Indies, ushered in the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>
and the European colonization of the Americas. Notable among them were: <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus (Cristoforo</color>
<color=#3366CC>Colombo)</color>, who discovered the New World and opened the Americas for European conquest; <color=#3366CC>John Cabot (Giovanni</color>
<color=#3366CC>Caboto)</color>, the first European to arrive in <color=#3366CC>Newfoundland</color>; <color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color> (for whom the Americas were named), who
demonstrated circa 1501 that the New World was not Asia but a previously unknown continent; and <color=#3366CC>Giovanni da</color>
<color=#3366CC>Verrazzano</color>, the first European to explore the Atlantic coast of <color=#3366CC>North America</color>.
The French Revolution and Napoleon
The <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color> began in 1789 and immediately found supporters among the Italian people. After the <color=#3366CC>French</color>
<color=#3366CC>king</color> was overthrown and France became a republic, secret clubs favouring an Italian republic were formed throughout
Italy. In 1796, <color=#3366CC>Napoleon Bonaparte</color> led a French army into northern Italy and drove out <color=#3366CC>its Austrian rulers</color>. Napoleon
made himself emperor in 1804; parts of northern and central Italy were unified under the name of the Kingdom of Italy,
with Napoleon as king, the rest was annexed by France. French domination, which lasted less than 20 years, brought
representative assemblies and new laws that were uniform across the country; for the first time since ancient Rome,
Italians from different regions were using the same money and served in the same army. Many Italians began to see
the possibility of a united Italy free of foreign control.
Italian unification and the Kingdom of Italy
In the aftermath of <color=#3366CC>Napoleon's defeat</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Congress of Vienna</color>, Italy came under control of the <color=#3366CC>Austrian Empire</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg dynasty</color>. Italian nationalist movements, led by reformers such as <color=#3366CC>Giuseppe Mazzini</color>, occurred in several
parts of the peninsula from the 1830s to 1849. The <color=#3366CC>Risorgimento</color> revolution of the 1850s was ultimately successful, and
on 17 March 1861, <color=#3366CC>Victor Emmanuel II</color> was proclaimed king of the Kingdom of Italy.
Italian troops occupied Rome in 1870, and in July 1871, it formally became the capital of the kingdom. <color=#3366CC>Pope Pius IX</color>, a
longtime rival of Italian kings, stated he had been made a "prisoner" inside the <color=#3366CC>Vatican</color> walls and refused to cooperate
with the royal administration. Only in 1929 did the pope accept the unified Italy with <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> as its capital.
The process of Italian unification was completed in <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, with the annexation of Trieste, Istria, <color=#3366CC>Trentino-Alto</color>
<color=#3366CC>Adige</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Zara</color>. After World War I, Italy emerged as one of the world's four great powers. In the decades following
unification, Italy began creating colonies in <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>, and under <color=#3366CC>Benito Mussolini</color>'s Fascist regime conquered <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>,
founding the <color=#3366CC>Italian Empire</color> in 1936. The population of Italy grew to 45 million in 1940 and the economy, which had
been based upon agriculture until that time, started its industrial development, mainly in northern Italy.
The Italian Republic
On 2 June 1946, Italy held its first free election after more than 20 years of Fascist rule. Italians chose to replace the
monarchy, which had been closely associated with <color=#3366CC>Fascism</color>, with a republic. They elected a Constituent Assembly of
anti-fascist representatives, which created a new democratic Italian constitution in 1947.
Under the Treaty of Peace with Italy, Yugoslavia annexed Istria, Kvarner, most of the Julian March, and <color=#3366CC>Zara</color>, which led
to the emigration of between 230,000 and 350,000 ethnic Italians, Slovenians, Croatians, and Istro-Romanians, who
chose to maintain Italian citizenship.
In 1949 Italy became a member of <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Marshall Plan</color> helped to revive the Italian economy which, until the late
1960s, enjoyed a period of sustained economic growth commonly called the "Economic Miracle". In 1957, Italy was a
founding member of the <color=#3366CC>European Economic Community</color> (EEC), which became the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> (EU) in 1993.
Ethnogenesis
Due to historic demographic shifts in the <color=#3366CC>Italian peninsula</color> throughout history, its geographical position in the center of
the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>, and Italy's regional ethnic diversity since ancient times, modern Italians are genetically diverse.
Bronze Age
Italians, like most Europeans, largely descend from three distinct lineages: Paleolithic <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>, such as the
Epigravettian culture, who arrived in the Italian peninsula as early as 35,000 to 40,000 years ago; Neolithic Early
European Farmers who migrated from <color=#3366CC>Western Asia</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic Revolution</color> 9,000 years
ago; and <color=#3366CC>Yamnaya</color> Steppe pastoralists who expanded into Europe from the Pontic–Caspian steppe of Ukraine and
southern Russia during the Indo-European migrations 5,000 years ago.

The first wave of <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color> migrations into Italy in the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> occurred from <color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color> (e.g. the <color=#3366CC>Bell</color>
<color=#3366CC>Beaker</color> culture), followed by the Italo-Celts (e.g. the Celtic-speaking Canegrate culture and the Italic-speaking
Proto-Villanovan culture, both deriving from the Proto-Italo-Celtic Urnfield culture). Recent DNA studies confirmed the
arrival of Steppe-related ancestry in Northern Italy to at least 2000 BCE and in Central Italy by 1600 BCE, with this
ancestry component increasing through time. In the late Bronze Age and early <color=#3366CC>Iron Age</color>, Celtic-speaking <color=#3366CC>La Tène</color> and
Hallstatt cultures spread over a large part of Italy, with related archeological artifacts found as far south as <color=#3366CC>Apulia</color>.
Italics occupied northeastern, southern, and central Italy. The "West Italic" group (including the Latins) were the first
wave. Major tribes included the Latins and Falisci in Lazio; the Oenotrians and Italii in <color=#3366CC>Calabria</color>; the Ausones, Aurunci
and Opici in <color=#3366CC>Campania</color>; and perhaps the Veneti in <color=#3366CC>Veneto</color> and the Sicels in Sicily. They were followed, and largely
displaced by the East Italic (Osco-Umbrians) group.
Iron Age
During the Iron Age, prior to Roman rule, Italy was predominantly inhabited by Italic tribes. The peoples living in the
area of modern Italy and the islands were:
• <color=#3366CC>Etruscans</color> (Camunni, Lepontii, Raeti);
• Sicani in <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>
• Elymians;
• Ligures (Apuani, Bagienni, Briniates, Corsi, Friniates, Garuli, Hercates, Ilvates, Insubres, Orobii, Laevi, Lapicini,
Marici, Statielli, Taurini);
• Italics (Latins, Falisci, Marsi, Umbri, Volsci, Marrucini, Osci, Aurunci, Ausones, Campanians, Paeligni, Sabines,
Bruttii, Frentani, Lucani, Samnites, Pentri, Caraceni, Caudini, Hirpini, Aequi, Fidenates, Hernici, Picentes, Vestini,
Morgeti, Sicels, Veneti);
• Iapygians (Messapians, Daunians, Peucetians);
• Celts (Allobroges, Ausones, Boii, Carni, Cenomani, Ceutrones, Graioceli, Lepontii, Lingones, Segusini, Senones,
Salassi, Veragri, Vertamocorii);
• <color=#3366CC>Greeks</color> of <color=#3366CC>Magna Graecia</color>;
• Sardinians (Nuragic tribes), in <color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color>
By the beginning of the Iron Age, the <color=#3366CC>Etruscans</color> had emerged as the dominant civilization on the Italian peninsula. The
Etruscans, expanded from Etruria over a large part of Italy, covering what is now <color=#3366CC>Tuscany</color>, western <color=#3366CC>Umbria</color>, and

northern <color=#3366CC>Lazio</color>, as well as what are now the Po Valley, <color=#3366CC>Emilia-Romagna</color>, south-eastern <color=#3366CC>Lombardy</color>, southern <color=#3366CC>Veneto</color>,
and western <color=#3366CC>Campania</color>. Ancient authors report several hypotheses for the origin of the Etruscans, including that they
came from the Aegean Sea. Modern archaeological and genetic research concluded that the Etruscans were
autochthonous and had a genetic profile similar to their Latin neighbors, notably lacking recent admixture with Anatolia
or the Eastern Mediterranean.
The Ligures were one of the oldest populations in Italy and Western Europe, possibly of Pre-Indo-European origin.
According to Strabo, they were not Celts but later became influenced by the Celtic culture of their neighbours, and thus
are sometimes referred to as Celticized Ligurians or Celto-Ligurians. Their language had similarities to both Italic (<color=#3366CC>Latin</color>
and the Osco-Umbrian languages) and <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color> (Gaulish). They primarily inhabited the regions of <color=#3366CC>Liguria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Piedmont</color>,

northern <color=#3366CC>Tuscany</color>, western <color=#3366CC>Lombardy</color>, western <color=#3366CC>Emilia-Romagna</color> and northern <color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color>, but are believed to have once
occupied an even larger portion of ancient Italy as far south as <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>. They were also settled in <color=#3366CC>Corsica</color> and in the
<color=#3366CC>Provence</color> region along the southern coast of modern <color=#3366CC>France</color>.
Beginning in the 8th century BCE, Greeks arrived in Italy and founded cities along the coast of southern Italy and
eastern Sicily, which became known as <color=#3366CC>Magna Graecia</color> ("Greater Greece"). The Greeks were frequently at war with the
native Italic tribes, but nonetheless managed to Hellenize and assimilate much of the indigenous population located
along eastern Sicily and the Southern coasts of the Italian mainland. According to Beloch, the number of Greek citizens
in southern Italy reached only 80,000 to 90,000 at most, while the local people subjected by the Greeks were between
400,000 and 600,000. By the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, Greek power in Italy was challenged and began to decline,
and many Greeks were pushed out of peninsular Italy by the native Oscan, Brutti, and Lucani tribes.
The <color=#3366CC>Gauls</color> crossed the Alps and invaded northern Italy in the 4th and 3rd centuries BC, settling in the area that became
known as Cisalpine Gaul. Although named after the Gauls, the region was mostly inhabited by indigenous tribes,
namely the Ligures, Etruscans, Euganei, and Veneti. Estimates by Beloch and Brunt suggest that in the 3rd century
BCE, Gaulish settlers in north Italy numbered between 130,000 and 140,000 out of a total population of about 1.4
million. The northern half of Cisalpine Gaul was already inhabited by the Celtic Lepontii since the Bronze Age.
Speaking about the Alpine region, the Greek historian <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color>, wrote:
The <color=#3366CC>Alps</color> are inhabited by numerous nations, but all <color=#3366CC>Keltic</color> with the exception of the Ligurians, and these, though of a
different race, closely resemble them in their manner of life.
According to <color=#3366CC>Pliny</color> and <color=#3366CC>Livy</color>, after the invasion of the Gauls, some of the Etruscans living in the Po Valley sought refuge
in the Alps and became known as the Raeti. The Raeti inhabited the region of <color=#3366CC>Trentino-Alto Adige</color>, as well as eastern
<color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tyrol</color> in western <color=#3366CC>Austria</color>. The Ladins of north-eastern Italy and the Romansh people of Switzerland are
said to be descended from the Raeti.
Roman
The <color=#3366CC>Romans</color> — who according to legend originally consisted of three ancient tribes: Latins, Sabines and Etruscans —
would go on to <color=#3366CC>conquer the whole Italian peninsula</color>. During the Roman period hundreds of cities and colonies were

established throughout Italy, including <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, <color=#3366CC>Turin</color>, Como, Pavia, <color=#3366CC>Padua</color>, <color=#3366CC>Verona</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vicenza</color>, <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color> and many
others. After the Roman conquest of Italy, "the whole of Italy had become Latinized". The Romans continued expansion
northward to conquer Cisalpine Gaul and establish colonies in the former Gallic territory, including <color=#3366CC>Bologna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Modena</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Reggio Emilia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Parma</color>, <color=#3366CC>Piacenza</color>, Cremona and <color=#3366CC>Forlì</color>. According to <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color>:
The Cispadane peoples occupy all that country which is encircled by the Apennine Mountains towards the Alps as far
as Genua and Sabata. The greater part of the country used to be occupied by the Boii, Ligures, Senones, and
Gaesatae; but since the Boii have been driven out, and since both the Gaesatae and the Senones have been
annihilated, only the Ligurian tribes and the Roman colonies are left.
The Boii, the most powerful and numerous of the Gallic tribes, were expelled by the Romans after 191 BCE and settled
in <color=#3366CC>Bohemia</color>, while the Insubres still lived in Mediolanum in the 1st century BCE.
Latin colonies were founded at <color=#3366CC>Ariminum</color> in 268 BCE and at Firmum in 264 BCE, while large numbers of Picentes, who
previously inhabited the region, were moved to Paestum and settled along the river Silarus in <color=#3366CC>Campania</color>. Between 180
and 179 BCE, 47,000 Ligures belonging to the Apuani tribe were removed from their home along the modern
Ligurian-Tuscan border and deported to Samnium, an area corresponding to inland Campania, while Latin colonies
were established in their place at <color=#3366CC>Pisa</color>, Lucca and Luni. Such population movements contributed to the rapid
Romanization and Latinization of Italy.
During the Imperial period, the dominant genetic trend for Rome and Central Italy was a notable shift towards Eastern
Mediterranean ancestry, with an increase in a Neolithic Iranian component of individuals in samples found in these
areas compared to those from the Bronze Age. Studies have found that there was considerably more genetic influence
from the Eastern Mediterranean than other parts of the Roman empire found in the Imperial Roman samples.
Middle Ages
A large Germanic confederation of Sciri, Heruli, Turcilingi, and Rugians, led by <color=#3366CC>Odoacer</color>, invaded and settled Italy in
476 CE. They were preceded by the Alemanni, including 30,000 warriors with their families, who settled in the Po
Valley in 371 CE, and by <color=#3366CC>Burgundians</color> who settled between Northwestern Italy and Southern France in 443 CE. The
Germanic tribe of the <color=#3366CC>Ostrogoths</color> led by <color=#3366CC>Theodoric the Great</color> conquered Italy and, in order to legitimize their rule to
Roman subjects who believed in the superiority of Roman culture over foreign "<color=#3366CC>barbarian</color>" culture, created a blended
Romano-Germanic culture. Since Italy had a population of several million, the Goths did not constitute a significant
addition to the local population: at most, several thousand Ostrogoths in a population of 6 or 7 million. After the <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color>, which devastated the local population, the Ostrogoths were defeated. Nevertheless, according to Roman historian
<color=#3366CC>Procopius of Caesarea</color>, the Ostrogothic population was allowed to live peacefully in Italy with their Rugian allies under
Roman sovereignty.
In the sixth century, another Germanic tribe known as the <color=#3366CC>Longobards</color> invaded Italy, which in the meantime had been
reconquered by the East Roman or Byzantine Empire. The Longobards were a small minority compared to the roughly
4 million inhabitants of Italy at the time. They were later followed by the Bavarians and the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color>, who conquered and
ruled most of Italy. Some groups of <color=#3366CC>Slavs</color> settled in parts of the northern Italian Peninsula between the 7th and 8th
centuries, while <color=#3366CC>Bulgars</color> led by Alcek settled in Sepino, Bojano, and Isernia. These Bulgars preserved their speech and
identity until the late 8th century.
Following Roman rule, Sicily, Corsica, and Sardinia were conquered by the <color=#3366CC>Vandals</color>, then by the Ostrogoths, and finally
by the Byzantines. Sicily was later invaded by the Arabs in the 9th century and the <color=#3366CC>Normans</color> in the 11th century,
leading to the formation of a unique Norman-Arab-Byzantine culture in Sicily. During the subsequent <color=#3366CC>Swabian</color> rule
under the Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Frederick II</color>, who spent most of his life as <color=#3366CC>king of Sicily</color> in his court in <color=#3366CC>Palermo</color>, Moors
were progressively eradicated until the massive deportation of the last <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color> of Sicily. As a result of the Arab
expulsion, many towns across Sicily were left depopulated. By the 12th century, <color=#3366CC>Swabian</color> kings granted immigrants

from northern Italy (particularly <color=#3366CC>Piedmont</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lombardy</color> and <color=#3366CC>Liguria</color>), Latium and <color=#3366CC>Tuscany</color> in central Italy, and <color=#3366CC>French</color>

<color=#3366CC>regions</color> of <color=#3366CC>Normandy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Provence</color> and <color=#3366CC>Brittany</color> (all collectively known as Lombards.) settlement into Sicily, re-establishing
the Latin element into the island, a legacy which can be seen in the many Gallo-Italic dialects and towns found in the
interior and western parts of Sicily, brought by these settlers. Before them, other Lombards arrived in <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>, with an
expedition departed in 1038, led by the Byzantine commander George Maniakes, which for a very short time managed
to snatch Messina and <color=#3366CC>Syracuse</color> from <color=#3366CC>Arab</color> rule. The Lombards who arrived with the Byzantines settled in Maniace,
Randazzo and Troina, while a group of <color=#3366CC>Genoese</color> and other Lombards from Liguria settled in Caltagirone. After the
marriage between the Norman Roger I of Sicily and Adelaide del Vasto, descendant of the Aleramici family, many
Northern Italian colonisers (known collectively as Lombards) left their homeland, in the Aleramici's possessions in
<color=#3366CC>Piedmont</color> and <color=#3366CC>Liguria</color> (then known as Lombardy), to settle on the island of Sicily. It is believed that the Lombard
immigrants in Sicily over a couple of centuries were a total of about 200,000. An estimated 20,000 Swabians and
40,000 <color=#3366CC>Normans</color> settled in the southern half of Italy during the 10th and 11th centuries. Additional Tuscan migrants
settled in Sicily after the Florentine conquest of Pisa in 1406.
Some of the Muslims expelled by the Normans were deported to Lucera (Lugêrah, as it was known in Arabic). Their
numbers eventually reached between 15,000 and 20,000, leading Lucera to be called Lucaera Saracenorum because it
represented the last stronghold of Islamic presence in Italy. The colony thrived for 75 years until it was sacked in 1300
by Christian forces under the command of the Angevin Charles II of Naples. The city's Muslim inhabitants were exiled
or sold into slavery. After the expulsions of Muslims in Lucera, Charles II replaced Lucera's Saracens with Christians,
chiefly <color=#3366CC>Burgundian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Provençal</color> soldiers and farmers, following an initial settlement of 140 Provençal families in 1273.
A remnant of the descendants of these Provençal colonists, still speaking a Franco-Provençal dialect, has survived until
the present day in the villages of Faeto and Celle di San Vito.
Modern period
Substantial migrations of Lombards to Naples, Rome, and Palermo continued in the 16th and 17th centuries, driven by
the constant overcrowding in the north. Minor but significant settlements of <color=#3366CC>Slavs</color> and Arbereshe in Italy have been
recorded, while Scottish soldiers – the Garde Ecossaise – who served the French King, <color=#3366CC>Francis I</color>, settled in the
mountains of <color=#3366CC>Piedmont</color>.
The geographical and cultural proximity with Southern Italy pushed Albanians to cross the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Otranto</color>, especially
after <color=#3366CC>Skanderbeg</color>'s death and the conquest of the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Ottomans</color>. In defense of the Christian religion and in
search of soldiers loyal to the Spanish crown, Alfonso V of Aragon, also king of Naples, invited Arbereshe soldiers to
move to Italy with their families. In return the king guaranteed to Albanians lots of land and a favourable taxation.
Arbereshe and Schiavoni were used to repopulate abandoned villages or villages whose population had died in
earthquakes, plagues and other catastrophes. Albanian soldiers were also used to quell rebellions in Calabria. Slavic
colonies were established in eastern Friuli, <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> and <color=#3366CC>Molise</color> (Molise Croats).
Between the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color> and the <color=#3366CC>early modern period</color>, there were several waves of immigration of Albanians into
Italy, in addition to another in the 20th century. The descendants of these Albanian emigrants, many still retaining the
<color=#3366CC>Albanian language</color>, the Arbëresh dialect, have survived throughout southern Italy, numbering about 260,000 people,
with roughly 80,000 to 100,000 speaking the Albanian language.
Italian Surnames
Most of Italy's surnames (cognomi), with the exception of a few areas marked by linguistic minorities, derive from
Italian. Many are derived from an individual's physical qualities (e.g. Rossi, Bianchi, Quattrocchi, Mancini, Grasso, etc.),
occupation (Ferrari, Auditore, Sartori, Tagliabue, etc.), fatherhood or lack thereof (De Pretis, Orfanelli, Esposito,
Trovato, etc.), and geographic location (<color=#3366CC>Padovano</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pisano</color>, Leccese, Lucchese, etc.). Some of them also indicate a
remote foreign origin (Greco, <color=#3366CC>Tedesco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Moro</color>, Albanese, etc.).
Italian diaspora
Italian migration outside Italy occurred over centuries in a series of migration cycles. A large diaspora took place after
Italy's unification in 1861 and continued through 1914 with the lead up to the <color=#3366CC>First World War</color>. One major motivation for
emigrants at this time was a post-unification economic slump within Italy (except for the "industrial triangle" between
<color=#3366CC>Milan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Turin</color>) that coincided with a boom in industrialization, urbanization, and economic expansion
elsewhere in the world, which provided better economic opportunities. Large-scale emigration continued through the
late 1920s, well into the Fascist regime, and a subsequent wave was observed after the end of the <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color>.
Another wave of migration outside Italy began in the 21st century and is still ongoing, caused by the debt crisis in Italy.
Over 80 million people claiming full or partial Italian descent live outside Italy. A majority of these, about 50 million total,
live in <color=#3366CC>South America</color>. Brazil has the largest number of Italian descendants outside Italy, and in Argentina, over 62.5%
of the country's population has at least one Italian ancestor. Another 23 million Italian descendants live in North
America (United States and Canada), 7 to 8 million in other parts of Europe (primarily in France, Germany, Switzerland,
and the United Kingdom), and another 1 million in Oceania (Australia and New Zealand). To a lesser extent, people of
full or partial Italian descent are also found in Africa (particularly in the former Italian colonies of Eritrea, Somalia, Libya,
and Ethiopia; and in others countries such as South Africa, Tunisia, and Egypt), in the Middle East (such as the United
Arab Emirates with 10,000 Italian immigrants), and in Asia (<color=#3366CC>Singapore</color> is home to a sizeable Italian community).
Culture
<color=#3366CC>Italy</color> is considered one of the birthplaces of <color=#3366CC>Western civilization</color> and has been described as a cultural superpower.
Italian culture is incredibly diverse, spanning the entire <color=#3366CC>Italian peninsula</color> plus <color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>. Italy was the origin of
phenomena of international impact including the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic Church</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Maritime republics</color>, <color=#3366CC>Romanesque art</color>, <color=#3366CC>Scholasticism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Rinascimento</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mannerism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Scientific</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Baroque</color>, <color=#3366CC>Neoclassicism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fascism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>European integration</color>.
Italy became a seat of learning in 1088 with the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>University of Bologna</color>, the first <color=#3366CC>university</color> and the
oldest in continuous operation. The Schola Medica Salernitana, in southern Italy, the first medical school in Europe,
and many other centers of higher education followed. The European <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> began in Italy and was powered by
leading Italian painters, sculptors, architects, scientists, literature authors, and music composers. Italy continued to
influence European cultural throughout the <color=#3366CC>Baroque</color> period and into the Romantic period, with a strong Italian presence
in music.
The country contains several world-famous cities. <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> was the capital of the ancient Roman Empire, the seat of the
Pope of the Catholic Church, and the capital of reunified Italy. <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> was the heart of the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>. <color=#3366CC>Turin</color>, which
used to be the capital of Italy, is a center of automobile engineering. <color=#3366CC>Milan</color> is the industrial and financial capital of Italy
and one of the world's fashion capitals. <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>'s intricate canal system attracts tourists from all over the world
especially during the Venetian Carnival and the Biennale. <color=#3366CC>Naples</color> has the largest historic city center in Europe and the
<color=#3366CC>world's oldest continuously active public opera house</color>. Due to its relatively late national unification and the historical
autonomy of the regions that comprise the Italian peninsula, many Italian traditions and customs can be identified by
their regions of origin.
Philosophy
<color=#3366CC>Italian literature</color> had a significant influence on Western philosophy, from the ancient Greeks and Romans, to the
Rinascimento, to the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>, to modern philosophy.
Medieval Italian philosophy was mainly influenced by Christianity. Saint <color=#3366CC>Thomas Aquinas</color> was a <color=#3366CC>Dominican</color> theologian,
experimentalist, and professor at the <color=#3366CC>University of Paris</color> from the Kingdom of Sicily. Aquinas was notable for introducing
a framework of <color=#3366CC>Aristotelian philosophy</color> to Christian theology.

Major Italian cities like <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, <color=#3366CC>Milan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>, <color=#3366CC>Padua</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bologna</color> and <color=#3366CC>Naples</color> – which hosted important universities and an
abundance of coffeeshops, which became hubs for intellectual conversation – were centers of scholarship in
Enlightenment Europe. Italy was the home of several important philosophers, such as <color=#3366CC>Giambattista Vico</color> (who is widely
considered the founder of modern Italian philosophy) and Antonio Genovesi; scientists such as <color=#3366CC>Alessandro Volta</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Luigi Galvani</color>; <color=#3366CC>Cesare Beccaria</color> (considered one of the fathers of classical criminal theory and modern <color=#3366CC>penology</color>, who
penned one of the earliest prominent condemnations of <color=#3366CC>torture</color> and th e<color=#3366CC>death penalty</color>).
Some of the most prominent philosophies and ideologies of the late 19th and 20th centuries were developed in Italy,

including <color=#3366CC>anarchism</color>, <color=#3366CC>communism</color>, <color=#3366CC>socialism</color>, <color=#3366CC>futurism</color>, <color=#3366CC>fascism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Christian democracy</color>. Some notable Italian
philosophers in the era include Antonio Rosmini, the founder of Italian idealism; <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Gentile</color>, an idealist and fascist
philosopher; and <color=#3366CC>Antonio Gramsci</color>, an important philosopher within <color=#3366CC>Marxist</color> and communist theory, credited with
creating the theory of cultural hegemony. <color=#3366CC>Italian fascism</color> was the official philosophy and ideology of the Italian
government from the 1920s to the 1940s led by Benito Mussolini.
Early Italian feminists include Sibilla Aleramo, Alaide Gualberta Beccari, and Anna Maria Mozzoni, although
proto-feminist philosophies had previously been explored by earlier Italian writers such as <color=#3366CC>Christine de Pizan</color>, Moderata
Fonte, and Lucrezia Marinella. Italian physician and educator <color=#3366CC>Maria Montessori</color> is credited with the creation of the
<color=#3366CC>Montessori philosophy of education</color>. <color=#3366CC>Giuseppe Peano</color> was one of the founders of <color=#3366CC>analytic philosophy</color> and contemporary
<color=#3366CC>philosophy of mathematics</color>. Italian analytic philosophers writing in the 21st century include Carlo Penco, Gloria Origgi,
Pieranna Garavaso and Luciano Floridi.
Literature
Formal Latin literature began in 240 BC, when the first stage play was performed in Rome. The Romans were famous
for their poets, dramatists, orators, philosophers, and historians; important figures included <color=#3366CC>Pliny the Elder</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pliny the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Younger</color>, <color=#3366CC>Virgil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Horace</color>, Propertius, <color=#3366CC>Ovid</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Livy</color>.
Saint <color=#3366CC>Francis of Assisi</color> is widely considered the first Italian poet, with his religious song Canticle of the Sun. Notable
poets in the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> include <color=#3366CC>Dante Alighieri</color>, <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Boccaccio</color>.
During the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, humanists such as Leonardo Bruni, Coluccio Salutati and <color=#3366CC>Niccolò Machiavelli</color> published
important histories and philosophical writings. Philosophers during the <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color>, such as Apostolo Zeno
and <color=#3366CC>Metastasio</color>, disseminated their ideas across Europe. <color=#3366CC>Carlo Goldoni</color>, a Venetian playwright and librettist, created
the comedy of character. The leading figure of the 18th-century Italian literary revival was Giuseppe Parini.
<color=#3366CC>Giacomo Leopardi</color> was an influential poet in the 19th century, known for his radical views. Italian novelists include
<color=#3366CC>Alessandro Manzoni</color>, author of the historical novel I promessi sposi ("The Betrothed"); <color=#3366CC>Italo Svevo</color>, author of <color=#3366CC>La</color>
<color=#3366CC>coscienza di Zeno</color>; <color=#3366CC>Luigi Pirandello</color>, winner of the 1934 Nobel Prize in Literature; and Federigo Tozzi and <color=#3366CC>Giuseppe</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ungaretti</color>, pioneers of <color=#3366CC>existentialism</color> in the European novel.
Modern literary figures and Nobel laureates include <color=#3366CC>Gabriele D'Annunzio</color>, nationalist poet <color=#3366CC>Giosuè Carducci</color>, realist

writer <color=#3366CC>Grazia Deledda</color>, theatre author <color=#3366CC>Luigi Pirandello</color>, short story writer <color=#3366CC>Italo Calvino</color>, poet <color=#3366CC>Salvatore Quasimodo</color>, poet
<color=#3366CC>Eugenio Montale</color>, <color=#3366CC>Umberto Eco</color>, and satirist and theatre author <color=#3366CC>Dario Fo</color>.
Politics
The <color=#3366CC>politics of Italy</color> are conducted through a parliamentary republic with a multi-party system. <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> has been a
democratic republic since 2 June 1946, when the monarchy was abolished by popular referendum. <color=#3366CC>Executive power</color> is
exercised by the Council of Ministers, which is led by the Prime Minister, officially referred to as "President of the
Council" (Presidente del Consiglio). <color=#3366CC>Legislative power</color> is primarily vested in the <color=#3366CC>two houses</color> of Parliament, but the
Council of Ministers can introduce bills and holds the majority in both houses. The judiciary is <color=#3366CC>independent</color> of the
executive and the legislative branches. The President presides over the High Council of the Judiciary as the <color=#3366CC>head of</color>
<color=#3366CC>state</color>, a position that is separate from all three branches.
The Presidents of Italy were Enrico De Nicola, Luigi Einaudi, Giovanni Gronchi, Antonio Segni, Giuseppe Saragat,
Giovanni Leone, Sandro Pertini, Francesco Cossiga, Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, Giorgio Napolitano
and Sergio Mattarella.
The legal and social status of Italian women has undergone rapid transformations and changes during the past
decades. This includes family laws, the enactment of anti-discrimination measures, and reforms to the penal code (in
particular with regard to crimes of violence against women). After World War II, women were given the right to vote in
1946 Italian institutional referendum. The new Italian Constitution of 1948 affirmed that women had equal rights. It was
not however until the 1970s that women in Italy scored some major achievements with the introduction of laws
regulating divorce (1970), abortion (1978), and the approval in 1975 of the new family code. Today, women have the
same legal rights as men in Italy, and have mainly the same job, business, and education opportunities.
Law and justice
Since the Roman Empire, most western contributions to Western legal culture was the emergence of a class of Roman
jurists. During the Middle Ages, <color=#3366CC>Saint Thomas Aquinas</color> integrated the theory of natural law with the notion of an eternal
and Biblical law. During the Renaissance, Professor <color=#3366CC>Alberico Gentili</color>, the founder of the science of <color=#3366CC>international law</color>,
authored the first treatise on public international law, and separated secular law from canon law and Catholic theology.
<color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>'s greatest legal theorists, <color=#3366CC>Cesare Beccaria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Giambattista Vico</color> and Francesco Mario Pagano, are
remembered for their legal works, particularly on criminal law. Francesco Carrara, an advocate of abolition of the death
penalty, was one of the foremost European criminal lawyers of the 19th century. During the last periods, numerous
Italians have been recognised as prominent prosecutor magistrates.
Economy
The <color=#3366CC>economy of Italy</color> is a <color=#3366CC>highly developed</color> social market economy. It is the third-largest national economy in the
<color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, the 10th-largest in the world by nominal GDP, and the 12th-largest by GDP (PPP). <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> is a founding
member of the European Union, the Eurozone, the <color=#3366CC>OECD</color>, the <color=#3366CC>G7</color> and the <color=#3366CC>G20</color>; it is the eighth-largest exporter in the
world, with $611 billion exported in 2021. Its closest trade ties are with the other countries of the European Union, with
whom it conducts about 59% of its total trade; Italy's largest trading partners, in order of market share in exports, are

<color=#3366CC>Germany</color> (12.5%), <color=#3366CC>France</color> (10.3%), the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> (9%), <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> (5.2%), the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> (5.2%) and <color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color>
In the post-World War II period, Italy saw a transformation from an agriculture-based economy, which had been
severely affected by the consequences of the <color=#3366CC>World Wars</color>, into one of the world's leading countries in <color=#3366CC>world trade and</color>
<color=#3366CC>exports</color>. Italy is the seventh-largest <color=#3366CC>manufacturing</color> country, characterised by many small and medium-sized enterprises,
with fewer global multinational corporations than other economies of comparable size. Italy is a large manufacturer and
exporter of <color=#3366CC>machinery</color>, <color=#3366CC>vehicles</color>, <color=#3366CC>pharmaceuticals</color>, furniture, food, clothing, and other products.
Noteworthy Italian entrepreneurs include Alessandro Martini, Luigi Lavazza, Pietro Ferrero, <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Agnelli</color>, Piero
Pirelli, Gaspare Campari, Adriano Olivetti, <color=#3366CC>Enzo Ferrari</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ferruccio Lamborghini</color>, Enrico Mattei, Luciano Benetton, and
Giovanni Rana.
Visual art
<color=#3366CC>Roman art</color> was influenced by <color=#3366CC>the art of ancient Greece</color>, but Roman painting does have unique characteristics. The only
surviving Roman paintings are <color=#3366CC>wall paintings</color>, many from villas in <color=#3366CC>Campania</color>, in Southern Italy. Such paintings can be
grouped into four main "styles" or periods and may contain the first examples of <color=#3366CC>trompe-l'œil</color>, pseudo-perspective, and
pure landscape. Panel painting became more common in Italy during the <color=#3366CC>Romanesque</color> period, under the heavy
influence of Byzantine <color=#3366CC>icons</color>. <color=#3366CC>Medieval art</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gothic painting</color> trended towards realism, with interest in the depiction of
volume and perspective, notably by <color=#3366CC>Cimabue</color> and then his pupil <color=#3366CC>Giotto</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color> is said by many to be the golden age of painting. In Italy, artists like <color=#3366CC>Paolo Uccello</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fra</color>

<color=#3366CC>Angelico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Masaccio</color>, <color=#3366CC>Piero della Francesca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Andrea Mantegna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Filippo Lippi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Giorgione</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tintoretto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sandro Botticelli</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Raphael</color>, <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Bellini</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Titian</color> developed refined drawing and painting
techniques through the use of <color=#3366CC>perspective</color> and the study of <color=#3366CC>human anatomy</color> and proportion. <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color> was active
as a sculptor from about 1500 to 1520, producing famous works such as his <color=#3366CC>David</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pietà</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Moses</color>. Other significant

Renaissance sculptors include <color=#3366CC>Lorenzo Ghiberti</color>, <color=#3366CC>Luca Della Robbia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Donatello</color>, <color=#3366CC>Filippo Brunelleschi</color> and <color=#3366CC>Andrea del</color>
<color=#3366CC>Verrocchio</color>.
In the 15th and 16th centuries, the High Renaissance gave rise to a stylised art known as <color=#3366CC>mannerism</color>. In place of the
balanced compositions and rational approach to perspective that characterised the early Renaissance, the Mannerists
sought instability, artifice, and doubt. The unperturbed faces and gestures of <color=#3366CC>Piero della Francesca</color> and the calm
Virgins of Raphael are replaced by the troubled expressions of <color=#3366CC>Pontormo</color> and the emotional intensity of <color=#3366CC>El Greco</color>.
17th century Italian Baroque painters include <color=#3366CC>Caravaggio</color>, <color=#3366CC>Annibale Carracci</color>, <color=#3366CC>Artemisia Gentileschi</color>, Mattia Preti, Carlo
Saraceni and Bartolomeo Manfredi. In the 18th century, French Rococo inspired the Italian Rococo movement, with
artists such as <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Battista Tiepolo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Canaletto</color>. <color=#3366CC>Antonio Canova</color>'s Italian Neoclassical sculpture focused on the
idealist aspect of the movement.
Some major Italian <color=#3366CC>Romantic</color> painters from the 19th century were <color=#3366CC>Francesco Hayez</color>, Giuseppe Bezzuoli and Francesco
Podesti. <color=#3366CC>Impressionism</color> was brought to Italy from France by the Macchiaioli movement, led by Giovanni Fattori and
Giovanni Boldini, and <color=#3366CC>Realism</color> style, led by Gioacchino Toma and Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo. In the 20th century,
Italian art was revolutionized by the <color=#3366CC>Futurism</color> movement, primarily through the sculptural works of <color=#3366CC>Umberto Boccioni</color>
and Giacomo Balla, and the metaphysical paintings of <color=#3366CC>Giorgio de Chirico</color>, who influenced later <color=#3366CC>Surrealist</color> artists like
Bruno Caruso and Renato Guttuso.
Music
Several instruments associated with <color=#3366CC>classical music</color>, including the piano and violin, were invented in Italy; and many of
the prevailing classical music forms, such as the <color=#3366CC>symphony</color>, concerto, and <color=#3366CC>sonata</color>, can trace their roots back to
innovations of 16th- and 17th-century Italian music. Italian opera was founded in the early 17th century in cities such as
<color=#3366CC>Mantua</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>, and has been influential on the Western opera tradition.
Notable Italians composers include <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina</color>; <color=#3366CC>Claudio Monteverdi</color>; the Baroque composers

Scarlatti, <color=#3366CC>Corelli</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Vivaldi</color>; the Classical composers <color=#3366CC>Paganini</color> and <color=#3366CC>Rossini</color>; and the Romantic composers <color=#3366CC>Bellini</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Donizetti</color>, <color=#3366CC>Verdi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Puccini</color>, whose operas, including <color=#3366CC>La bohème</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tosca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Madama Butterfly</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Turandot</color>, are among
the most frequently worldwide performed in the standard repertoire. In the Post Romantic era, the composer <color=#3366CC>Ottorino</color>
<color=#3366CC>Respighi</color> was also recognized internationally for his symphonic tone poems: Pines of Rome, Fountains of Rome and
Roman Festivals. Modern Italian composers such as <color=#3366CC>Berio</color>, Maderna, and Nono proved significant in the development
of <color=#3366CC>experimental</color> and <color=#3366CC>electronic music</color>.
Starting in the late 19th century, Italians also emerged as notable <color=#3366CC>conductors</color> and musical directors of operatic and
symphonic orchestras on the international concert hall stage. Included among them were: <color=#3366CC>Arturo Toscanini</color>, and Victor
de Sabata,. In the modern era, several others followed their lead including: <color=#3366CC>Claudio Abbado</color>, Riccardo Chailly, <color=#3366CC>Carlo</color>
<color=#3366CC>Maria Giulini</color>, Fabio Luisi, Riccardo Muti, and Gianandrea Noseda,. Others achieved international acclaim as principal
orchestral musicians including Ernesto Köhler, Leonardo De Lorenzo.
<color=#3366CC>Jazz</color> found a particularly strong foothold among Italians in the 1920s and remained popular despite the xenophobic
cultural policies of the Fascist regime. Later, Italy embraced the <color=#3366CC>progressive rock</color> movement of the 1970s, with bands
like PFM and Goblin, as well as <color=#3366CC>disco</color> and <color=#3366CC>electronic music</color>. Italo disco, characterised by a futuristic sound and
prominent usage of synthesizers and <color=#3366CC>drum machines</color>, was one of the earliest electronic dance genres and influenced
Euro disco. <color=#3366CC>Giorgio Moroder</color>, three-time <color=#3366CC>Academy Award</color> winner, was highly influential in the development of <color=#3366CC>EDM</color>.
Italian <color=#3366CC>pop music</color> is represented annually with the Sanremo Music Festival, which served as inspiration for the
<color=#3366CC>Eurovision</color> song contest, and the Festival of Two Worlds in Spoleto. Singers such as pop diva <color=#3366CC>Mina</color>, classical crossover
artist <color=#3366CC>Andrea Bocelli</color>, <color=#3366CC>Grammy</color> winner <color=#3366CC>Laura Pausini</color>, and European chart-topper <color=#3366CC>Eros Ramazzotti</color> have attained
international acclaim.
Theatre and dance
The traditions of Italian theatre have their origins in the <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek</color> colonies of <color=#3366CC>Magna Graecia</color> in Southern Italy and
the theatre of the Italic peoples and <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>. During the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, Italian theatre was expansive, comprising
the dramatization of Catholic liturgies, the court performances of jesters, the songs of <color=#3366CC>troubadours</color>, and public city
festivals. <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> theatre was marked by a resurgence of the classics; ancient theatrical texts were re-discovered,
translated from Latin to Italian, and performed. The cities of <color=#3366CC>Ferrara</color> and <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> played a prominent role in the
rediscovery and renewal of theatrical art in the fifteenth century.
From the 16th to 18th century, <color=#3366CC>commedia dell'arte</color> was a popular form of <color=#3366CC>improvisational theatre</color>. Traveling troupes of
players would set up an outdoor stage and provide entertainment in the form of <color=#3366CC>juggling</color>, <color=#3366CC>acrobatics</color>, and humorous
plays called canovaccio. Actors improvised the performance from loose scenarios called lazzi, that provided the basic
situation and plot. Actors relied on a repertoire of <color=#3366CC>stock characters</color>, such as foolish old men, devious servants, or
military officers full of false <color=#3366CC>bravado</color>.
Noteworthy Italian theater actors and playwrights are Jacopone da Todi, Angelo Beolco, <color=#3366CC>Isabella Andreini</color>, <color=#3366CC>Carlo</color>
<color=#3366CC>Goldoni</color>, Eduardo Scarpetta, Ettore Petrolini <color=#3366CC>Eleonora Duse</color>, Eduardo De Filippo, Carmelo Bene and Giorgio Strehler.
The <color=#3366CC>ballet</color> dance genre also originated in Italy. It began during the Italian Renaissance as a form of entertainment at
court weddings. At first, ballets were woven into the midst of an opera, providing the audience a moment of relief from
the opera's dramatic intensity. By the 17th century, Italian ballets were performed in their entirety in between the acts of
an opera, and had become a popular dance form in their own right by the 1800s.
Cinema
The history of <color=#3366CC>Italian cinema</color> began in the late 1800s, a few months after the <color=#3366CC>Lumière brothers</color> started motion picture
exhibitions. The first Italian director was Vittorio Calcina, a collaborator of the Lumières, who filmed <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo XIII</color> in
1896. In the 1910s the Italian film industry developed rapidly. Cabiria, a 1914 Italian <color=#3366CC>epic film</color> directed by Giovanni
Pastrone, is considered the most famous Italian <color=#3366CC>silent film</color>. It was also the first film in history to be shown in the <color=#3366CC>White</color>
<color=#3366CC>House</color>. The oldest European <color=#3366CC>avant-garde</color> cinema movement, Italian futurism, took place in the late 1910s. After a
period of decline in the 1920s, the Italian film industry was revitalized in the 1930s with the arrival of sound film. Popular
Italian genres during this period were the Telefoni Bianchi, consisting of comedies with glamorous backgrounds, and
Calligrafismo, with its artistic, highly formalistic, and <color=#3366CC>expressive</color> styling.
Italian film was widely renowned after the end of <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>. Notable Italian film directors from this period include

<color=#3366CC>Vittorio De Sica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Federico Fellini</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sergio Leone</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pier Paolo Pasolini</color>, <color=#3366CC>Luchino Visconti</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo Antonioni</color>, Dussio
Tessari, and <color=#3366CC>Roberto Rossellini</color>; some of these are recognised among the greatest and most influential filmmakers of

Science and technology

Italy is home to the greatest number of <color=#3366CC>UNESCO</color> <color=#3366CC>World Heritage Sites</color> (61 total) and half of the world's great art

Cuisine
<color=#3366CC>Italian cuisine</color> is a <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean cuisine</color> consisting of the ingredients, recipes, and cooking techniques developed
across the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color> since antiquity, and later spread around the world together with waves of Italian diaspora.
Italian cuisine includes deeply rooted traditions common to the whole country, as well as regional cuisines which are in
continuous exchange.
One of the main characteristics of Italian cuisine is its simplicity, with many dishes made up of few ingredients, and
therefore Italian cooks often rely on the quality of the ingredients, rather than the complexity of preparation. The most
popular dishes and recipes, over the centuries, have often been created by ordinary people moreso than by chefs,
which is why many Italian recipes are suitable for home and daily <color=#3366CC>cooking</color>.
Noteworthy Italian chefs include Bartolomeo Scappi, Gualtiero Marchesi, Lidia Bastianich, Antonio Carluccio, Cesare
Casella, Carlo Cracco, Antonino Cannavacciuolo, Gino D'Acampo, Gianfranco Chiarini, Massimiliano Alajmo, Massimo

Baiji
The baiji (Lipotes vexillifer) is a possibly <color=#3366CC>extinct</color> species of <color=#3366CC>river dolphin</color> native to the <color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color> river system in China. It is
thought to possibly be the first <color=#3366CC>dolphin</color> species driven to extinction due to the impact of humans. This dolphin is listed
as "critically endangered: possibly extinct" by the IUCN, has not been definitively seen in over 20 years, and several
surveys of the Yangtze have failed to find it. The species is also called the Chinese river dolphin, Yangtze river dolphin,
Yangtze dolphin, and whitefin dolphin. The genus name Lipotes means "left behind" and the species epithet vexillifer
means "flag bearer". It is nicknamed the "Goddess of the Yangtze" and was regarded as the goddess of protection by
local fishermen and boatmen. It is not to be confused with the Chinese white dolphin (Sousa chinensis) or the <color=#3366CC>finless</color>
<color=#3366CC>porpoise</color> (Neophocaena phocaenoides). This is the only species in the genus Lipotes.
The baiji population declined drastically in decades as China industrialized and made heavy use of the river for fishing,
transportation, and <color=#3366CC>hydroelectricity</color>. Following surveys in the Yangtze River during the 1980s, the baiji was claimed to
be the first dolphin species in history driven to extinction by humans. A Conservation Action Plan for Cetaceans of the
Yangtze River was approved by the Chinese Government in 2001. Efforts were made to conserve the species, but a
late 2006 expedition failed to find any baiji in the river. Organizers declared the baiji functionally extinct. The baiji
represents the first documented global extinction of an aquatic "<color=#3366CC>megafaunal</color>" vertebrate in over 50 years since the
demise of the Japanese sea lion (Zalophus japonicus) and the Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis) in the
1950s. It also signified the disappearance of an entire mammal family of river dolphins (Lipotidae). The baiji's extinction
would be the first recorded extinction of a well-studied <color=#3366CC>cetacean</color> species (it is unclear if some previously extinct
varieties were species or subspecies) to be directly attributable to human influence. The baiji is one of a number of
extinctions to have taken place due to the degradation of the Yangtze, alongside that of the Chinese paddlefish, as well
as the now extinct in the wild Dabry's sturgeon.
Swiss economist and CEO of the baiji.org Foundation August Pfluger funded an expedition in which an international
team, taken in part from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Fisheries Research Agency in
Japan, searched for six weeks for signs of the dolphin. The search took place almost a decade after the last exploration
in 1997, which turned up only 13 of the cetaceans.
In August 2007, a Chinese man reportedly videotaped a large white animal swimming in the Yangtze. Although the
animal was tentatively identified as a baiji, the presence of only one or a few animals, particularly of advanced age, is
not enough to save a functionally extinct species from true extinction. The last known living baiji was Qi Qi, who died in
2002. The <color=#3366CC>World Wildlife Fund</color> is calling for the preservation of any possible baiji habitat, in case the species is located
and can be revived.
Anatomy and morphology
Baiji were thought to breed in the first half of the year, the peak calving season being from February to April. A 30%
pregnancy rate was observed. Gestation would last 10–11 months, delivering one calf at a time; the interbirth interval
was 2 years. Calves measured around 80 – 90 cm at birth, and nursed for 8–20 months. Males reached sexual maturity
at age four, and females at age 6. Mature males were about 2.3 m (7.5 ft) long, females 2.5 m, with the longest
specimen 2.7 m. The animal weighed 135 – 230 kg, with a lifespan estimated at 24 years in the wild. The Yangtze river
dolphin was pale blue to grey on the dorsal (back) side, and white on the ventral (belly) side. It had a long and slightly
upturned beak with 31–36 conical teeth on either jaw. Its dorsal fin was low and triangular in shape and resembled a
light-colored flag when the dolphin swam just below the surface of the murky <color=#3366CC>Yangtze River</color>, hence the name
"white-flag" dolphin. It had smaller eyes compared to oceanic dolphins.
When escaping from danger, the baiji can reach 60 km/h, but usually stays within 30 to 40 km/h. Because of its poor
vision, the baiji relies primarily on sonar for navigation. The sonar system also plays an important role in socializing,
predator avoidance, group coordination, and expressing emotions. Sound emission is focused and highly directed by
the shape of the skull and melon. Peak frequencies of echolocation clicks are between 70 kHz and 100 kHz.
Distribution
Historically, the baiji occurred along 1,700 km of the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze, from <color=#3366CC>Yichang</color> in the west
to the mouth of the river near to <color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color>, as well as in <color=#3366CC>Poyang</color> and <color=#3366CC>Dongting</color> Lakes and the smaller Qiantang River to
the south. This had been reduced by several hundred kilometres both upstream and downstream, and was limited to
the main channel of the Yangtze, principally the middle reaches between the two large tributary lakes, Dongting and
Poyang. Approximately 12% of the world's human population lives and works within the Yangtze River catchment area,
putting pressure on the river.
Evolutionary history
The baiji is not closely related to any living species of dolphin, having diverged from the ancestors of the La Plata
dolphin and <color=#3366CC>Amazon river dolphin</color> during the Miocene, estimated to be around 16 million years ago. The closest known
relative of the baiji is Parapontoporia, native to the western coast of North America during the Latest <color=#3366CC>Miocene</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Pliocene</color>. The baiji was one of five species of dolphins known to have made <color=#3366CC>fresh water</color> their exclusive habitat. The
<color=#3366CC>other five species</color>, including the boto and the La Plata dolphin, have survived in the <color=#3366CC>Río de la Plata</color> and <color=#3366CC>Amazon</color> rivers
in <color=#3366CC>South America</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and <color=#3366CC>Indus</color> rivers on the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>.
It is well known that the river dolphins are not a natural group. Their mitochondrial genome reveals a split of two
separate lineages, Platanista and Lipotes + (Inia + Pontoporia), having no sister relationship with each other, and the
Platanista lineage is always within the <color=#3366CC>odontocete</color> clade instead of having a closer affinity to <color=#3366CC>Mysticeti</color>. The position of
the Platanista is more basal, suggesting separate divergence of this lineage well before the other one. The Lipotes has
a sister relationship with Inia + Pontoporia, and they together formed the sister group to the Delphinoidea. This result
strongly supports paraphyly of the classical river dolphins, and the nonplatanistoid river dolphins do represent a
monophyletic grouping, with the Lipotidae as the sister taxa to (Iniidae + Pontoporiidae), and is well congruent with the
studies based on short interspersed repetitive elements (SINEs).
Low values of haplotype diversity and nucleotide diversity were found for the baiji of the Yangtze River. The analysis of
molecular variance (AMOVA) supported a high level of overall genetic structure. The males having a higher genetic
differentiation than the females suggested a significant female-biased dispersal.
The aquatic adaptations of the baiji and other cetaceans have happened slowly and can be linked to positively selected
genes (PSGs) and/or other functional changes. Comparative genopic analyses have uncovered that the baiji have a
slow molecular clock and molecular adaptations to their aquatic environment. This information leads scientists to
conclude that a bottleneck must have occurred near the end of the last deglaciation, a time that coincided with rapid
temperature decrease and a rise in eustatic sea level. Scientists have also looked into PSGs in the baiji genome which
are used for DNA repair and response to DNA stimulus. These PSGs have not been found in any other mammal
species. Pathways being used for DNA repair have been known to have a major impact on brain development and
have been implicated in diseases including microcephaly. The slow down of the substitution rate among cetaceans may
have been affected by the evolution of DNA damage pathways. Over time, river dolphins, including the baiji, have had a
reduction in the size of their eyes and the acuity of their vision. This probably stems from poor visibility in fluvial and
estuarine environments. When analyzing the baiji genome, scientists have found that there are four genes that have
lost their function due to a frameshift mutation or premature stop codons. The baiji has the lowest single-nucleotide
polymorphism (SNP) frequency reported thus far among mammals. This low frequency could be related to the relatively
low rate of molecular evolution in cetaceans; however, considering that the decrease in the rate of molecular evolution
in the baiji was not as great as the decrease in heterozygosity rate, it is likely that much of the low genetic diversity
observed was caused by the precipitous decline in the total baiji population in recent decades and the associated
breedings.
The reconstructed demographic history over the last 100,000 years featured a continual population contraction through
the last glacial maximum, a serious bottleneck during the last deglaciation, and sustained population growth after the
eustatic sea level approached the current levels. The close correlation between population trends, regional
temperatures, and eustatic sea levels suggest a dominant role for global and local climate changes in shaping the
baiji's ancient population demography.
Folklore
Per Chinese folklore, a beautiful young girl is said to have lived with her stepfather on the banks of the river Yangtze.
He was evil, a greedy man out for his own self-interest. One day, he took the girl on a boat, intending to sell her on the
market. Out on the river, though, he became infatuated with her beauty and tried to take advantage of her. But she
freed herself by plunging into the river, whereupon a big storm came and sank the boat. After the storm had thus
settled, people saw a beautiful dolphin swimming – the incarnation of the girl – which became known as the "Goddess
of the Yangtze". The baiji, in the region of Yangtze, is regarded as a symbol of peace and prosperity.
